The West Comes to Town
It is a rare occurrence indeed when an Execu
tive Council member living in the West is able
to participate actively in the affairs of this ad
ministrative body. Because it is so important
that the West be closely involved with Fraterni
ty direction, all cheered when Norman J.
Schoonover, Theta Theta '46, responded to an
invitation to serve with, "Have pin. Will
travel."
Thereupon, at a general meeting of the 137th
Convention held with the Beta Beta Chapter in
Hartford, Connecticut on August 22, 1980, this
resident of Boise, Idaho was elected to a twoyear term on the Executive Council. Brother
Schoonover's unswerving dedication to Psi Up
silon, his wide range of experience, and his
no-nonsense, get-it-done attitude soon made
him an integral member of the "team."
On November 20, 1981, only fifteen months
after joining the governing body ofthe Fraterni
ty, Brother Schoonover was elected unanimous
ly to serve as a Vice President of the Executive
Council, an honor which he enthusiastically
accepted. He already has proven himself
eminently qualified to handle this responsibil
ity.
Born in Spokane, Washington on April 13,
1924, Norm Schoonover moved to Boise, Idaho
in 1934, where he graduated from Boise High
School. He entered the University of Washing
ton in the fall of 1942 and was initiated into the
Theta Theta Chapter of Psi Upsilon Fraternity
on January 30, 1943.
Brother Schoonover's college career shortly
thereafter was interrupted by this country's in
volvement in World War II. He entered the
United States Army in 1943, serving variously
in three different branches �
the Infantry, En
gineers, and Signal Corps. While carrying out
his Signal Corps duties in Europe, Norm
Schoonover was a member of the "original cast"
in the Battle of the Bulge in the Ardennes.
Following his discharge from the Army in
November, 1945, Brother Schoonover returned
to the University of Washington to resume his
studies. While there his contributions to Psi
Upsilon's twenty-sixth Chapter were
many and
varied. The respect in which he was held by his
brothers was evidenced by the fact that he held
virtually every oflfice in the Theta Theta Chap
ter, including that of President in 1947.
It is hardly surprising that the success of the
1947 Convention, hosted by the Theta Theta
Chapter, was due in large part to the efforts ofits
Undergraduate Chairman, who was none other
than Norman J. Schoonover. At the closing ban
quet he led his Chapter in a choral arrangement
of a new Psi U song entitled "The Sweetheart
Song," which he and Dale O. Richardson, Theta
Theta '48 had collaborated in writing.
Upon graduating from the University of
Washington in 1948 with a degree in Econom
ics, Brother Schoonover became associated
with the Idaho First National Bank, initially
serving as branch manager. He continued his
studies, receiving a master's degree in banking
from the University of Washington in 1955.
Moving up to the responsibilities of an execu
tive oflficer in short order, he opted for semiretirement in 1973. Three years earher he had
been named a director of the bank, where he
still serves on the Loan Committee of the Board
of Directors.
Throughout his successful business career Fsi
U never has been forgotten. For several years
the relative newcomer to the Executive Council
has been a member of the Board of Directors of
the Psi Upsilon Alumni Association ofWashing
ton. Along with his membership in several so
cial organizations, Norm Schoonover finds time
to serve on the Board of Directors of the local
Boise hospital and to indulge in golf and travel,
his favorite pastimes.
Norm Schoonover, father of six and grand
father of four, is indeed a man of whom Psi
Upsilon can be proud. We are privileged to
have him assume a
leadership role in guiding
our
Fraternity.

Gamma Tau Chapter Adopts
Coat-of-Arms
Most fratemities have but one coat-ofarms, with no special emblems or sym
bols for the various chapters. Psi Upsilon
is one of the few who have chosen to
employ one international coat-of-arms
and a similar yet distinctive crest for each
of its Chapters.
On August 23, 1980 the official coat-ofarms for the Gamma Tau Chapter, de
signed by John C. white, Gamma Tau 74
and reviewed by Murray L. Eskenazi,
Lambda '56, was adopted by unanimous
approval of the 137th Convention, upon
the recommendation of the Gamma Tau
Chapter. The crest follows the standard
format as presented in the Annals of Psi
Upsilon .
The Chapter motto is Gnothoi Teknos
(rvuSois TeKvoa), which loosely trans
lates to "We understand work." The let
ters gamma and tau refer to the Chapter
name and to the Georgia Institute of
Technology. The long struggle of the
Chapter to build a new breed of "fraterni
ty" on the campus is reflected in the mot
to, which represents the Chapter's found
ing principles; working in academics, ser
vice, and social awareness. The Gamma
Tau's brotherhood is the most prized fruit
Coat-of-arms for the Gamma Tau Chap
ter, designed by John C. White, Gamma
Tau '74, and executed by Murray L.
Eskenazi, Lambda '56.
of the working effort.
The Owl of Psi Upsilon sits atop the
braided cord. Colors of the traditional Psi
U six braids are for Georgia Tech: antique
gold and white. White in heraldry nor
mally is meant to be unplaited metal or
silver, so that the gold and white of Geor
gia Tech is then gold and silver.
Shields of the crests for Psi Upsilon
Chapters are to be alternately gold or
silver; hence the Gamma Tau is silver in
the rotation for a background. Because of
the symmetry of the symbol to represent
the Gamma Tau, a half shield of gold Psi
Upsilon on black background was chosen.
The gold wheel as the symbol for the
Chapter takes on a dual meaning: I) the
wheel is one of the heraldic symbols for
labor and 2) it symbolizes technology and
knowledge. The cogwheel is an accepted
modem heraldic symbol, and it is the
background symbol on the Georgia Tech
seal. The heraldic wheel has eight spokes.
Because the Gamma Tau was the thirtyfourth Chapter of the Fratemity to re
ceive a charter, a 34-cog wheel was
chosen; however, only seventeen are
seen. The wheel's gold color against the
silver (white) background again serves as
a reminder of Georgia Tech's colors.
The men of the Gamma Tau can be
proud of their new coat-of-arms, a symbol
of their aims, aspirations, and achieve
ments.
Niagara Frontier Alumni Association Holds Founders' Day Dinner
On Thursday evening, October 26,
1981, the Niagara Frontier Alumni Asso
ciation of Psi Upsilon Fraternity held its
annual Founders' Day Dinner at the
Orchard Park Country Club in Orchard
Park, New York. There was no dampen
ing of spirits despite the rain-out of the
planned golf outing. The renewing of old
friendships and making of new ones com
bined to provide a most enjoyable even
ing.
Arthur A. Buss, Jr., Epsilon Omega
'64, was re-elected President of the Asso
ciation for the coming year. Also re
elected were Vice President David M.
Sisson, Upsilon '72, and Secretary James
M. Dunnigan, Upsilon '73. Newly
elected as Treasurer was Barry W. Mallon, Gamma '44.
The immediate past Treasurer,
Richard S. Kurtz, Phi '39, was honored
for fourteen years of accurate service. His
father, Howard W. Kurtz, Pi '12, was one
of the founders of the Niagara Frontier
alumni group. Sewell F. Hubbard, Epsi
lon Phi '38, was appointed official associa
tion photographer.

The Saga of the Missing Pin
The story of the recovery of a Psi Up
silon badge more than forty years after it
was lost is one of the most remarkable
series ofcircumstances which has come to
the attention of the Fraternity Office in
recent years. Portions ofcorrespondence
in the files describe the unfolding events
dramatically .

November 4, 1965
Dear Brother Fretz:
An interesting thing happened tonight
here in Waterloo, Ontario while I was
looking at some of my landlord's memen
toes. He took out a pin and asked me ifl
knew what it was. You can imagine my
surprise when I saw that it was one of our
pins.
He told me that he was working in a
parking lot in Kitchener, Ontario before
the war (World War II). One night he
noticed two couples looking on the
ground for something. The next night he
noticed the pin on the ground and re
membered that the car had American
license plates. He put the pin away and
never thought of it again until we noticed
it tonight. That was 27 years ago!
You probably have access to the names
of all the brothers. Would you see
whether you could find out anything
about the present whereabouts ofa David
S. Woods?
Bill Beach
November 18, 1965
Dear Mr. Beach:
We were most interested to read of
your discovery of the Psi U badge belong
ing to David S. Woods. He is a member of
the Psi Chapter, Class of 1939.
Unfortunately we have had Mr. Woods
marked "address unknown" since June,
1961. However, we will certainly pursue
the matter.
Norah G. Cleather
November 29, 1965
Dear Mr. Beach:
We are so sorry to tell you that we have
been unable to track down an address for
Mr. David S. Woods.
Should we ultimately get an address for
him, we will certainly let you know.
Norah G. Cleather
July 17, 1980
Dear Brother Beach;
While going through the archives in
preparation for updating a history of Psi
Upsilon for our 1983 Sesquicentennial
Anniversary, I came across the enclosed
set of correspondence. By checking our
records I found that we now have David
S. Woods' address. I don't know if you
still have his pin, but I think it would be a
tremendous thing to reunite the two
again, if you have not already done so.
I am not writing to Brother Woods yet,
as I would like to leave that pleasure to
you.
Michael J. Crane
August 12, 1980
Dear Brother Woods:
I enclose herewith a
photocopy of a
letter recently received from Michael J.
Crane, as well as copies of earher corres
pondence.
I still have your pin and will mail it to
you once you confirm receipt of this let
ter.
William Gordon Beach
September 1, 1980
Dear Brother Beach;
What a wonderful surprise it was to
receive your letter and learn that my
fratemity pin had been found and that
you have it. Naturally I had long ago
given up any hope of recovering it. Psi
Upsilon means a great deal to me and is a
family affair as well. My father, Stanley T.
Woods, Psi '13 and my brother Richard S.
Woods, Upsilon '41 are both fraternity
brothers. So naturally I am
highly pleased
at the thought of getting it back.
My recollection of the circumstances
under which the pin was lost are a bit hazy
in my mind. However, since I've never
had the pleasure of visiting Kitchener,
Ontario personally, someone must have
"borrowed" it for some festive occasion in
Kitchener and lost it there.
The most interesting and impressive
aspect of this whole affair is the interest of
the several Psi U brothers who have
helped to find me and see to it that my pin
is returned. That, I think, attests most
graphically to the fellowship and brother
ly spirit of the Fraternity. Though we are
all virtual strangers, the fraternal bond
has brought us together in a happy com
mon endeavor. My grateful thanks ex
tends to all involved, especially to
Brothers Beach and Crane.
The enclosed check is intended both to
express my gratitute for your interest and
thoughtfulness and to cover the expenses
you have incurred in trying to find me and
see to it that my pin is returned. I sincere
ly hope that the opportunity will arise so
that I may perform a similar service to a
brother Psi U.
Dave Woods
September 25, 1980
Dear Brother Woods:
I was pleased to receive your letter
dated September 1st, 1980 and to read
that you are interested in getting your pin
back.
I cashed the check and sent $10.00 to
the daughter of my former landlord who
died this year as his or her share in the
reward, and I am sending $10.00 to Mr.
Crane by way of a donation to the
Fraternity.
I enclose herein your pin.
Bill Beach
October 1, 1980
Dear Brother Beach:
Michael J. Crane has completed his
summer responsibilities as archivist and
has returned to his family's home in Lom
bard, Illinois.
In his behalf I do want to express our
sincere appreciation for your continuing
thoughtfulness. Your check will have spe
cial meaning as the first contribution to
our 1980-81 Annual Giving program.
Henry B. Poor

1980-81 Annual Giving Results Best Ever
The alumni of Psi Upsilon once again have come
through with a remarkable response to the Fraternity's
annual appeal for financial support. During the 1980-81
Annual Giving campaign 1,921 donors contributed
$76,291, topping the previous year's record high of
$71,695 by $4,596. This represents an average gift of
$39.71, up almost $4 from the 1979-80 average of
$35.78, due to the dramatic increase in leadership con
tributors, from 466 in 1979-80 to 566 in 1980-81.
The following statistics and lists serve to honor the
loyal members of Psi U who, by their generosity, have
helped to augment the services available to undergradu
ates and to perpetuate what is recognized as one of the
finest fraternities. Years of consecutive giving are shown
in parentheses after the name and class of donors in the
complete list of membership contributors. Names in
bolder print represent leadership contributors.
The Executive Council is deeply and profoundly grate
ful for each and every gift. Nowwemustaskouralumnito
dig a little deeper to meet the never-ending, always esca
lating need. The response to date of the 1981-82 cam
paign has been heartening indeed, but we need $83,800
in alumni contributions to balance the Fraternity's
budget. We think we can meet the challenge!

spring. By joining together for meals, we

brotherhood.
